question.problem:
$$

$$

Consider the vector $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ By evaluating the following quadratic forms at $x$ **only,** determine which of them **cannot** be positive-definite.

I. $R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$

II. $S(x)={x}^{T}\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]x$

III. $T(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$
question.worked_solution:
A quadratic form $Q(x)$ is positive-definite if $Q(x)>0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\}.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the quadratic forms by substituting $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]:$

- Quadratic form I *might* be positive-definite. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot (-3) \\  & =1+9+6 \\  & =16>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form II *might* be positive-definite. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =16>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form III *cannot* be positive-definite since

$$
\begin{aligned}T(x) & ={1}^{2}-(-3)^{2}+1\cdot (-3) \\  & =1-9-3 \\  & =-11<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."
